items.x_text:
Operation Snowball: Malbear Labs found a jailbroken DeepSeek Flash agent that ran a 2-week intrusion on a European telecom, starting with Cisco BroadWorks flaw CVE-2026-20320 (fixed in August). ~78,000-char prompt; no refusals recorded.

#AISecurity #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
A 78,000-character jailbreak. Then an AI agent ran an intrusion for two weeks. 🤖

What Infosecurity Magazine reported (9 Nov), from Malbear Labs research:
→ Malbear found the attacker's exposed working directory: 70+ session transcripts and the agent's own reports
→ The agent ran on DeepSeek Flash. A ~78,000-character prompt told it to treat any refusal as a malfunction; no refusals were recorded
→ Target: a European telecom (not named) and organisations hosted in its data centres. Way in: CVE-2026-20320, an unauthenticated XXE in Cisco BroadWorks that Cisco fixed in August
→ A Chinese-speaking operator checked in with short orders like "Go on" and "Stop". Malbear did not link it to a state actor
→ The agent reported credentials, private keys and billing records. These are the agent's own claims; Malbear didn't say whether victims confirmed them

The defender's lesson: AI makes old, patched flaws cheaper to exploit at scale. Patch KEV-listed bugs fast, treat internet-facing end-of-life JBoss 6 servers as compromised, and watch for tunnelling between internal hosts, not just at the edge.

cover.hook: An AI platform says attackers reached customer datasets and model weights.
cover.sub: Fireworks AI widened the scope of its October incident. It came in through a third-party cloud provider.

slides.title: How they got in
slides.body: Fireworks says a third-party cloud provider hosting its R&D machines had a security incident on 23 Oct. On 24 Oct the attacker used that access to reach Fireworks development machines and ran an unauthorized workload. It was detected the same day.

slides.title: What was reached
slides.body: Account and billing information: billing and shipping addresses, invoices, balances and credit usage. For a limited set of accounts: stored secrets, datasets and a subset of incomplete model weights. Fireworks says it doesn't store card numbers.

slides.label: the day the attacker reached Fireworks development machines, one day after the cloud provider's own incident
slides.note: Fireworks updated its bulletin on 9 Nov

slides.title: What it says wasn't hit
slides.body: Fireworks says it has seen no impact to Inference, the Training SDK or Nexus, which are zero data retention by default. It links the activity to the financially motivated "LLMJacking" group and has Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 on the forensics.

slides.title: If you use AI platforms
items: Rotate any API keys or secrets you stored with the platform
Know which datasets and fine-tunes you've uploaded, and where
Ask vendors who hosts their R&D and dev machines
Prefer zero-data-retention modes for sensitive data

What Fireworks AI said in its updated bulletin (9 Nov):
→ A third-party cloud provider hosting Fireworks R&D machines had a security incident on 23 Oct
→ On 24 Oct the attacker used that access to reach Fireworks development machines and ran an unauthorized workload; detected the same day
→ Account and billing information was affected: addresses, invoices, balances, credit usage. Card numbers aren't stored by Fireworks
→ For a limited set of accounts: stored secrets, datasets and a subset of incomplete model weights
→ No impact seen on Inference, the Training SDK or Nexus (zero data retention by default). Unit 42 is investigating; Fireworks links it to the "LLMJacking" group

The defender's lesson: what you upload to an AI platform is part of your attack surface. Rotate secrets you stored there, keep an inventory of datasets and fine-tunes you've shared, and ask vendors where their dev machines live.

items.x_text:
N-able N-central: a researcher published 30+ alleged zero-days with PoC code, unannounced. N-able took Hosted N-central offline on 9 Nov and told on-prem customers to take servers offline. No exploitation seen so far, it says.

#ZeroDay #CyberSecurity
items.ig_caption:
30+ zero-days published overnight. By Monday, the cloud platform was offline. 🔌

What BleepingComputer reported (9 Nov):
→ Researcher Sean Bales published more than 30 alleged zero-days in N-able N-central, a remote monitoring and management tool used by MSPs, with proof-of-concept code, late on Sunday 8 Nov
→ He didn't warn N-able first, saying earlier reports in another N-able product went unpatched. He says the work was AI-assisted
→ The reported flaws include authentication bypasses, XXE and remote code execution
→ N-able took Hosted N-central offline on 9 Nov and told on-prem customers to take servers offline until further notice
→ N-able: "we have not observed active exploitation". A hotfix is in progress; BleepingComputer hasn't verified every flaw

Why it matters: an RMM tool can push commands to every machine it manages. If your IT is outsourced, ask your MSP whether N-central is in the chain, and follow N-able's status page for the hotfix.

cover.hook: A securities regulator confirms its users' data leaked. Tax ID numbers included.
cover.sub: The Philippine SEC says names, contact details, birth dates and TINs may be exposed. It hasn't said how many users.

slides.title: What the SEC confirmed
slides.body: The Philippines' Securities and Exchange Commission sent users an advisory confirming a data breach on its digital platforms, days after the group Deep Web Konek flagged a possible breach of SEC-related user accounts.

slides.title: What may be exposed
slides.body: Full name, username, email, mobile number, date of birth, gender, address and TIN (tax identification number) of individual accounts. The SEC says no passwords leaked, no data was altered and no company records were involved.

slides.label: types of personal data the SEC says may have been exposed, including the tax ID number
slides.note: Total number of affected users not yet released

slides.title: How, per the SEC
slides.body: The advisory says accounts may have leaked through malware infection or unauthorized access by a third-party threat actor. The SEC notified the National Privacy Commission, reset credentials and tightened access controls.

slides.title: If you have an account
items: Change your SEC portal password, and anywhere you reused it
Run a full security scan on your devices
Expect calls and texts quoting your TIN and birth date
The SEC says it never asks for passwords or PINs

items.x_text:
GPUStack CVE-2026-102895 (CVSS 9.8): versions before 2.2.0 treat requests that look like localhost as the admin. Exploited in the wild and now on CISA KEV. Upgrade, recreate the container, revoke unknown admin API keys.

#PatchNow #AISecurity
items.ig_caption:
Look like localhost, and the AI cluster makes you admin. Now exploited. 🖥️

What's reported:
→ GPUStack, an open-source GPU cluster manager for serving AI models, has CVE-2026-102895 (CVSS 9.8)
→ Before 2.2.0, a request that appears to come from 127.0.0.1 is treated as the built-in admin; a same-host reverse proxy can make remote requests look local (Ostorlab, 5 Nov)
→ An admin can create persistent API keys, read worker and cloud secrets, and run code on worker hosts
→ The advisory says it was exploited in the wild against a v2.1.1 deployment; CISA has added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list (nFlo, 9 Nov)
→ The fix, 2.2.0, has been out since June

Patch now: upgrade to 2.2.0+ and recreate the container (pulling the image alone keeps the old process running). Then review admin users, API keys and inference backends, revoke anything unknown, and rotate worker and cloud credentials. Upgrading doesn't remove keys an attacker already made.
